title: As one who in his journey bates at Noone (lines added in 1674)
short: The first five lines of Book XII were added in 1674, when the original tenth book was divided; Michael pauses 'betwixt the world destroy'd and world restor'd'.
body: In the first edition of 1667, Michael's prophecy ran without a break from the covenant after the Flood ('Both Heav'n and Earth, wherein the just shall dwell') into 'Thus thou hast seen one World begin and end'. For the twelve-book edition of 1674 Milton divided that book and added five lines (12.1-5), printed here in square brackets: 'As one who in his journey bates at Noone, Though bent on speed, so heer the Archangel paus'd Betwixt the world destroy'd and world restor'd'. Verity explains the history and glosses 'bates' as 'slackens' or 'abates' (some editors read 'baits', to stop for refreshment). The simile of a traveller pausing at noon fits Michael's narrative journey through history and marks the midpoint between the old world and the new.

title: Nimrod: A mightie Hunter ... from Rebellion shall derive his name
short: Michael's account of Nimrod, the 'mighty hunter before the Lord' (Genesis 10:9), as the first tyrant and founder of monarchy: Milton's republicanism in biblical form.
body: After the Flood men live in 'fraternal state' until 'one ... of proud ambitious heart' arises who 'Will arrogate Dominion undeserv'd Over his brethren'. He is never named, but he is Nimrod, 'A mightie Hunter ... before the Lord' (Genesis 10:9), 'hunting (and Men not Beasts shall be his game)'. Verity explains that Milton reads 'hunter' as warrior and tyrant, following Josephus, and quotes Milton's Commonplace Book: Nimrod founded 'the Lordly Monarchy', 'a great Hunter, an Hebraisme for a Great Theife'. 'From Rebellion shall derive his name' plays on a supposed derivation from Hebrew marad, 'to rebel'; Verity notes the sarcasm, since the first king is himself the rebel, an answer to royalist charges against the regicides. The Dartmouth edition cites James I's theory of divine right, which 'from Heav'n claming second Sovrantie' mocks.

title: the Tower ... and the work Confusion nam'd (Babel)
short: Nimrod's followers build the tower of Babel with bitumen 'from the mouth of Hell'; God confounds their language, and the work is named 'Confusion'.
body: Nimrod's crew find 'The Plain, wherein a black bituminous gurge Boiles out from under ground, the mouth of Hell', and build 'a Citie and Towre, whose top may reach to Heav'n' (Genesis 11:4). Verity notes that Genesis does not connect Nimrod with the Tower, but that Josephus (Antiquities 1.4.2-3) and Dante do, and that bitumen was the mortar of Babylon. God sends 'a various Spirit to rase Quite out thir Native Language'; 'great laughter was in Heav'n' (Psalm 2:4) at the 'jangling noise'. 'Confusion nam'd' translates Genesis 11:9, where the margin explains Babel as 'Confusion'; Verity adds that the native etymology was 'gate of God'. Michael never names Nimrod or Babel, as the Dartmouth edition notes. The scene parallels the building of Pandaemonium (1.710-30).

title: since thy original lapse, true Libertie Is lost, which alwayes with right reason dwells Twinn'd
short: Michael explains that political tyranny follows inner tyranny: when reason is enslaved to passion, God permits outward tyrants. Liberty and right reason are twins.
body: Adam condemns Nimrod for claiming authority over men that God gave him only over beasts. Michael agrees, but adds that 'since thy original lapse, true Libertie Is lost, which alwayes with right reason dwells Twinn'd, and from her hath no dividual being': when men let 'upstart Passions' rule reason, God 'subjects him from without to violent Lords', so 'Tyrannie must be, Though to the Tyrant thereby no excuse' (12.83-96). Verity links the association of freedom with reason to 3.108-10 and 9.351-52, glosses 'right reason' (recta ratio) and 'Twinn'd', and hears Matthew 18:7 in 'must be'. The argument is Milton's explanation of the failure of the English republic: a people unfit for liberty receives servitude. The Dartmouth edition notes that the following lines on the curse of Ham were used to justify slavery.

title: Abraham: Ur of Chaldaea ... in his Seed All Nations shall be blest
short: Abraham, raised among idolaters, leaves Ur at God's call in faith; the promise that all nations will be blessed in his seed points to Christ.
body: Michael tells of 'one faithful man', Abraham, 'bred up in Idol-worship' beyond the Euphrates (Joshua 24:2-3), called to leave his father's house and go to a land he would be shown (Genesis 12:1-3). Verity explains that 'Hebrew' was thought to mean 'living across' the Euphrates, and notes the geographical confusions in Milton's 'Ur of Chaldaea, passing now the Ford To Haran': Milton, following Acts 7:2-4 and imperfect seventeenth-century maps, seems to place Ur in upper Mesopotamia. 'I see him, but thou canst not, with what Faith He leaves his Gods' echoes Hebrews 11:8, 'by faith Abraham ... went out, not knowing whither he went'. The promise that 'in his Seed All Nations shall be blest' is read, as the Dartmouth edition notes, as a prophecy of Christ (Galatians 3:16).

title: This River-dragon tam'd at length ... the Sea ... as on drie land between two christal walls
short: Pharaoh, the 'River-dragon' of Ezekiel 29:3, is humbled by the plagues; the Red Sea divides into 'two christal walls' for Israel and drowns his army.
body: Michael summarises the plagues of Egypt and calls Pharaoh 'This River-dragon', from Ezekiel 29:3, 'Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers', as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note; Verity explains that 'dragon' renders the Hebrew tannin, any monster. The sea 'Swell[s] ... in two christal walls' (12.197), a phrase Verity compares with Milton's own paraphrase of Psalm 136, 'The floods stood still, like walls of glass'. Pharaoh's army is drowned, fulfilling the simile of the Red Sea and 'Busiris and his Memphian Chivalrie' in Book I (1.306-11), where the fallen angels lay like the Egyptian corpses. The pillar of cloud and fire and the march through the wilderness follow Exodus 13-14.

title: by types And shadows ... From shadowie Types to Truth, from Flesh to Spirit
short: Michael explains typology: the Law of Moses, its sacrifices and its leaders are 'shadowie Types' foreshadowing Christ, who fulfils and replaces them.
body: God gives Israel laws and sacrifices 'informing them, by types And shadows, of that destind Seed to bruise The Serpent' (12.232-35). The Law cannot remove sin, 'for Law can discover sin, but not remove' (12.290); it serves to lead men 'From shadowie Types to Truth, from Flesh to Spirit, From imposition of strict Laws, to free Acceptance of large Grace, from servil fear To filial, works of Law to works of Faith' (12.303-06). Verity identifies the Pauline texts behind the passage, especially Romans, Galatians and Hebrews 10:1 ('the law having a shadow of good things to come'). The Dartmouth edition explains typology as a Protestant form of allegory, cites the scholarship of Madsen and Lewalski, and criticises its supersessionist treatment of Judaism. Moses himself is a type of the Mediator (12.240-44).

anchor: Joshua whom the Gentiles Jesus call
title: But Joshua whom the Gentiles Jesus call
greek: Hebrew Yehoshua, 'the Lord saves'; Greek Iêsous
short: Moses cannot bring Israel into the Promised Land; Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus, does: a type of Christ leading mankind to rest.
body: Moses, 'though of God Highly belov'd', may not lead Israel into Canaan (Deuteronomy 34), 'But Joshua whom the Gentiles Jesus call, His Name and Office bearing, who shall quell The adversarie Serpent, and bring back Through the worlds wilderness long wanderd man Safe to eternal Paradise of rest'. Verity explains that Joshua and Jesus are the same name, Greek Iēsous in the Septuagint, meaning 'the Saviour', and that Hebrews 4:8 treats Joshua as a type of Christ; he quotes Christian Doctrine 1.26: Moses, a type of the law, could not bring Israel into Canaan, 'but an entrance was given to them under Joshua, or Jesus'. The law (Moses) can lead to the border of rest; only grace (Jesus) can bring men in.

title: The seed of Woman: Virgin Mother, Haile
short: Michael announces the incarnation: the promised Seed will be born of a virgin, and Adam, overjoyed, at last understands the curse on the serpent.
body: The promise of 10.181 is fulfilled: from David's line will come a king 'of the most High', born of a virgin, 'The seed of Woman: Virgin Mother, Haile, High in the love of Heav'n'. Michael repeats Gabriel's greeting to Mary (Luke 1:28; Verity cites 1:28 and the Dartmouth edition 1:31-35), which Raphael had already applied to Eve as 'second Eve' (5.385-87). Verity compares the account of the nativity with the Nativity Ode and Paradise Regained (1.242-54). Adam rejoices, 'now clear I understand What oft my steddiest thoughts have searcht in vain', but imagines the victory as a physical duel; Michael corrects him: 'Dream not of thir fight, As of a Duel' (12.386-87), since the Son will conquer 'Not by destroying Satan, but his works In thee and in thy Seed' (12.394-95).

title: O goodness infinite ... full of doubt I stand, Whether I should repent me now of sin ... or rejoyce
greek: Latin O felix culpa, 'O happy fault' (Exsultet)
short: Adam wonders whether to repent his sin or rejoice in it, since it occasions so much greater good: the paradox of the 'fortunate fall'.
body: Hearing of the resurrection and final judgment, Adam exclaims: 'O goodness infinite, goodness immense! That all this good of evil shall produce, And evil turn to good ... full of doubt I stand, Whether I should repent me now of sin By mee done and occasiond, or rejoyce Much more, that much more good thereof shall spring, To God more glory, more good will to Men From God, and over wrauth grace shall abound' (12.469-78). The thought recalls the Easter Exsultet's 'O felix culpa' ('O happy fault, which merited such and so great a Redeemer') and Romans 5:20, 'where sin abounded, grace did much more abound', which the Dartmouth edition cites. A. O. Lovejoy's essay 'Milton and the Paradox of the Fortunate Fall' (1937) made the passage central to criticism. Note that Adam stays 'full of doubt': the poem does not simply endorse the paradox.

title: Wolves shall succeed for teachers, grievous Wolves
short: Michael foretells the corruption of the Church after the apostles: hirelings who turn religion to lucre and ambition and join it to secular power.
body: After the apostles 'Wolves shall succeed for teachers, grievous Wolves, Who all the sacred mysteries of Heav'n To thir own vile advantages shall turne Of lucre and ambition'. Verity quotes Paul's warning, 'after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you' (Acts 20:29), cross-refers to the 'lewd Hirelings' of 4.193 and the 'hireling wolves' of Milton's sonnet to Cromwell, and suggests that the passage (12.507-37) is aimed chiefly at the Church of England. Milton's targets are a paid clergy, unscriptural traditions, the union of church and 'secular power' (Verity cites Of Reformation and Dante's condemnation of papal temporal power), and the forcing of conscience: true worship is 'in Spirit and Truth' (John 4:23), and the Spirit's 'living Temples' are believers (1 Corinthians 3:16-17).

anchor: A Paradise within thee, happier farr
title: then wilt thou not be loath To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess A Paradise within thee, happier farr
short: Michael's final lesson: knowledge must be joined to faith, virtue, patience, temperance and love, which will give Adam an inner paradise happier than Eden.
body: Adam declares what he has learned: 'Henceforth I learne, that to obey is best', and that God works 'by small Accomplishing great things'. Michael approves, and tells him to add to knowledge 'Deeds to thy knowledge answerable, add Faith, Add Vertue, Patience, Temperance, add Love, By name to come call'd Charitie' (a list from 2 Peter 1:5-7, as the Dartmouth edition notes), 'then wilt thou not be loath To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess A Paradise within thee, happier farr'. Verity notes that the thought inverts Satan's 'my self am Hell' (4.75) and the idea that the mind is its own place (1.254-55), and that the 'top of Speculation' is the hill of vision (Latin specula, watch-tower). The inner paradise is the poem's answer to the loss in its title.

anchor: By mee the Promis'd Seed shall all restore
title: Eve's last words: thou to mee Art all things under Heav'n ... By mee the Promis'd Seed shall all restore
short: Eve, taught by God in a dream, speaks the last human words of the poem: she will go with Adam, and through her the promised Seed will restore all.
body: Eve wakes from a dream sent by God ('For God is also in sleep, and Dreams advise', 12.611, which recalls the Homeric idea that dreams come from Zeus, Iliad 1.63) and speaks: 'In mee is no delay; with thee to goe, Is to stay here; without thee here to stay, Is to go hence unwilling; thou to mee Art all things under Heav'n, all places thou'. Verity notes the echo of Virgil, 'in me mora non erit ulla' (Eclogues 3.52), and that Eve has taken to heart Michael's words that where God is, there is home (11.290-92). She ends: 'though all by mee is lost, Such favour I unworthie am voutsaft, By mee the Promis'd Seed shall all restore'. The Dartmouth edition observes that she has the gist rather than the precise theology; yet her words balance the poem's first line.

title: The brandisht Sword of God ... Fierce as a Comet ... the Libyan Air adust
short: The cherubim descend to guard Paradise; the flaming sword of Genesis 3:24 blazes before them like a comet, scorching the air like the Libyan desert.
body: The cherubim glide down 'as Ev'ning Mist Ris'n from a River o're the marish glides', and 'The brandisht Sword of God before them blaz'd Fierce as a Comet; which with torrid heat, And vapour as the Libyan Air adust, Began to parch that temperat Clime'. The image is Genesis 3:24: God placed 'Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life'. Verity notes Dunster's suggestion of Sylvester's Du Bartas, where the sword shines 'Like flaming comet in the midst of night', recalls the comet simile for Satan (2.708-11), and glosses 'adust' (scorched) and 'Libyan' as typical of heat; he also hears Lot's rescue from Sodom, when the angels took Lot and his wife by the hand (Genesis 19:16), in Michael's leading of Adam and Eve. The mist simile echoes Satan's creeping approach as 'a black mist low creeping' (9.179-80).

anchor: The World was all before them
title: The World was all before them ... They hand in hand with wandring steps and slow, Through Eden took thir solitarie way
short: The final lines: Adam and Eve weep, then go out into the world, free to choose, with Providence as guide, hand in hand yet solitary.
body: 'Som natural tears they drop'd, but wip'd them soon; The World was all before them, where to choose Thir place of rest, and Providence thir guide: They hand in hand with wandring steps and slow, Through Eden took thir solitarie way'. Verity notes that 'all the world's my way' in Mowbray's farewell (Richard II 1.3.206-07) has been compared, and records the old debate about the last couplet: Addison wished to omit it as too sad for an epic ending, and Bentley wrote a cheerful substitute, but most readers find the balance of loss and hope exact. The phrasing gathers the poem's themes: 'choose' recalls free will, 'wandring' recalls the devils' 'wandring mazes' (2.561) as the Dartmouth edition notes, and 'hand in hand' answers Eve's withdrawal of her hand in Book IX. Wordsworth opened The Prelude with an echo of the second line.
